Thank you for submitting your article "The role of the NMD factor UPF3B in olfactory sensory neurons" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Didier Stainier as the Senior and Reviewing Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: David M Bedwell (Reviewer #1); Luis R Saraiva (Reviewer #2).

While the revised manuscript was found to be much improved, there are several remaining issues that should be addressed.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, the authors examined the role of the NMD factor UPF3B in olfactory neurogenesis. They identified stage-specific olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) cell clusters in WT mice and found that UPF3B loss resulted in changes in the proportion of these cell clusters. They also identified a number of interesting UPF3B-dependent NMD target transcripts in vivo using single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis, including strong candidates with roles in olfactory neurogenesis, and neural development. Finally, they showed that UPF3B dampens the expression of a large cadre of anti-microbial genes and promotes the selection of specific olfactory receptor (Olfr) genes. This study provides important new insights into the olfactory field and identifies an important new post-transcriptional regulator that shapes OSN gene expression and OSN development.

Overall, this is an interesting manuscript with exciting new insights into the role of UPF3B in regulating gene expression in OSN cell clusters. The authors adequately addressed each of my previous concerns.

Reviewer #2:

The authors have made improvements in the manuscript, but unfortunately, they have not convincingly addressed some of my major concerns. Below I am detailing my responses to the rebuttal letter point by point:

1) No more comments. This concern is addressed.

2.1) The authors then present "two lines of evidence against a significant subsampling bias in their samples: First, each sample was pooled from 3 mice. Second, most samples had a similar percentage of OMP-YFP+ cells (between 5-7%)".

Unfortunately, without knowing the numbers of cells sorted in each sample, I am failing to see how any of these two reasons argue against it. The olfactory epithelium of young adult mice (8-10 weeks) is populated on average by ~10 million mature OSNs (mOSNs). If each sample contains on average 10,000 sorted cells, that would capture only 0.1% of all mOSNs. If each sample contains 100,000 sorted cells, that would still only make up 1% of all mOSNs, and so on. Since the authors "did not make note of the output cell number" in each sample, how could pooling animals or sorting similar percentages of cells between animals be used as an argument against subsampling? Also, only 4/8 of their samples had between 5-7% of sorted OMP-YFP+ cells, which is not "most samples". I am assuming the authors kept the FACS files, and thus should be able to retrieve those values. Is this the case?

Finally, what is the logic underlying the following statement: "We note that our manuscript is currently ~30% over the word limit."?

2.2) The authors here claim that they asked, "what genes are regulated by a particular factor in mOSNs" and that "the depth of RNA-seq analysis we used was sufficient to draw several conclusions". One of the unexpected major conclusions of the authors is that "over half of the downregulated genes in Upf3-null mOSNs are Olfr genes" and state that they "regard this finding as a robust result, as the RNA-seq coverage for Upf3b-null and control OSNs was 95.8% and 96.0%, respectively, of all annotated Olfr gene".

Since Olfr and many other genes are expressed zonally in the olfactory epithelium (PMID: 7812149, 15814789, 12709059, 32209480, etc), differences in dissection between animals could easily account for the differences observed in the RNA-seq data from sorted cells. Thus, showing the gene expression distribution of all Olfr genes for each of the sorted samples is a key QC step for this study and it should feature early on in the main figures. The authors should include that in the main text and present a plot containing the mean gene expression values (in log10) for all annotated mouse Olfr in either descending or ascending order for the WT and KO, include similar plots in supplementary for each individual sample and include all the gene names (and not just Ensembl IDs) in the “TPM” sheet of Supplementary file 1 to make this accessible to the community. It would also be very useful to present in supplementary a Venn diagram comparing all the Olfrs expressed in WT vs KO mice.

3) The Materials and methods are now much improved. Only one minor comment here: the authors should include the commercial source of the coyote and bobcat urines.

4) As I mentioned in my original comment, as Gap43 and Krt5 are not expressed in mature OSNs, they should not be called “olfactory neuronal markers”. Instead, Gap43 is a canonical marker for immature neurons and Krt5 a canonical marker for horizontal basal cells. In line with this, the authors do mention that "mOSN marker gene, Omp, is enriched in these mOSN samples, and that the non-mOSN markers genes, Krt5 and Lgr5, are de-enriched in these samples". Finally, the authors mention that their RNA-seq analysis was done "purified mOSNs, not whole OE". I was indeed aware of this, as it is was already explicit in the manuscript. I suggested plotting something similar to Figure 1C in PMID: 31392275, for 2 main reasons: i) it summarizes in one plot the gene expression levels for the canonical markers for all major cell types populating the olfactory epithelium, and ii) it visually allows the reader assess the levels of “contamination/hitchhiking” by other cell types during the sorting procedure.

Please correct this by specifically stating the cell types that those genes are indicative of (also, by “de-enriched” I assume the authors mean “depleted”?).

4.1) The Omp expression data should feature in Figure 1B, as it is the best canonical marker for mOSNs (also see previous response). It is well established that Omp and Gnal are expressed ubiquitously in the majority of mOSNs across all the olfactory epithelium, so I do not see how that could be an explanation.

4.2) No more comments. This concern is addressed.

5) Regarding Figure 6—figure supplement 1B in the revised manuscript: HBCs and GBCs are not OSNs, and it is incorrect to refer them as such. Only immature and mature OSNs should be called OSNs. Please correct this in the figures and throughout the text. Also, on the right-hand panel of Figure 6—figure supplement 1B it would be useful to list all the other cell types that make up 100%.

6) No more comments. This concern is addressed.

7) Olfr genes are expressed zonally in the olfactory epithelium (PMID: 7812149, 15814789, 12709059, 32209480, etc) and differences in dissection between animals could easily translate into differential expression artifacts. Moreover, different mouse strains express different Olfrs at different levels (PMID: 28438259). Since the authors i) have not yet convincingly addressed my previous concerns about a potential bias in dissection (see above), ii) the mice used in this studies were on mixed or different genetic backgrounds, and iii) one of the major claims of the authors is that half of the differentially expressed genes are Olfrs; the authors should validate at least their top 2 differentially expressed Olfrs across the two genotypes.

8) This comment is addressed.

Reviewer #3:

The authors have done an excellent job revising this manuscript. The revised submission is significantly improved. I have no further comments. The manuscript should be accepted as it is.

claims.source: In contrast, the low-translation group of mRNAs exhibited no correlation between their translation rate and NMD magnitude (R2 = 0.06; Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of translation efficiency and NMD magnitude for high-confidence NMD targets.

claims.claim: The vast majority of mRNAs were similarly translated in both Upf3b-null and WT mOSNs.
claims.source: When we plotted the TE of mRNAs when expressed in Upf3b-null mOSNs vs. when expressed in WT mOSNs, we found that the vast majority of mRNAs were similarly translated in both genetic backgrounds, as measured by RiboTag analysis (Figure 2H, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on RiboTag analysis comparing translation efficiency in Upf3b-null and WT mOSNs.

claims.claim: Only 16 mOSN mRNAs had a significant change in translation efficiency as a result of Upf3b loss.
claims.source: Only 16 mOSN mRNAs migrated off the diagonal and thus had a significant change in TE as a result of Upf3b loss (Figure 2H,I).
claims.evidence: This is based on RiboTag analysis comparing translation efficiency in Upf3b-null and WT mOSNs.

claims.claim: After filtering, 25,165 cells remained for scRNA-seq analysis.
claims.source: After filtering out poor quality cells, 25,165 cells remained for subsequent analysis.
claims.evidence: This is based on quality control filtering of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Using UMAP, 16 known cell types in the OE were identified.
claims.source: Using a nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique—uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)—we identified cell clusters corresponding to 16 known cell types in the OE (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on UMAP analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Re-clustering of OSN precursors/OSNs revealed several cell sub-clusters within each of the HBC, GBC, iOSN, and mOSN stages.
claims.source: Re-clustering of OSN precursors/OSNs (HBCs, GBCs, iOSNs, and mOSNs) revealed several cell sub-clusters within each of these four stages (Figure 3D,E).
claims.evidence: This is based on re-clustering analysis of scRNA-seq data for OSN lineage cells.

claims.claim: Cell-cycle analysis showed that all four HBC sub-clusters primarily contain quiescent cells, while the GBC sub-clusters have many cells that are proliferating.
claims.source: Consistent with this, cell-cycle analysis showed that all four HBC sub-clusters primarily contain quiescent cells, while the GBC sub-clusters have many cells that are proliferating (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is based on cell cycle analysis of scRNA-seq data using cell cycle gene expression.

claims.claim: Monocle pseudotime trajectory analysis suggested that the four GBC sub-clusters have a linear developmental relationship, with GBC-1 the most immature, GBC-2 more advanced, and GBC-3 and −4 the most advanced.
claims.source: Monocle pseudotime trajectory analysis suggested that these four sub-clusters have a linear developmental relationship, with GBC-1 the most immature, GBC-2 more advanced, and GBC-3 and −4 the most advanced (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is based on Monocle trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Most WT mOSNs segregated into three different cell clusters.
claims.source: Most WT mOSNs segregated into three different cell clusters (Figure 3D), each of which preferentially express different genes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of scRNA-seq data for mOSNs.

claims.claim: Monocle pseudotime analysis indicated that OSN precursor/OSN cell clusters follow a HBC→GBC→iOSN→mOSN trajectory.
claims.source: Monocle pseudotime analysis of the OSN precursor/OSN cell clusters indicated that they follow a HBC→GBC→iOSN→mOSN trajectory (Figure 5A), consistent with previous studies (Fletcher et al., 2017; Schwob et al., 2017; Tepe et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is based on Monocle trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data and is consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in the frequency of HBCs in Upf3b-null mice relative to WT mice (p<0.05).
claims.source: scRNA-seq analysis revealed that there was a significant reduction in the frequency of HBCs in Upf3b-null mice relative to WT mice, when compared to either all OSN precursors/OSNs or all OE cells (p<0.05; Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data comparing cell frequencies between genotypes.

claims.claim: The density of TRP63+ cells was significantly less in Upf3b-null OE than WT OE.
claims.source: As validation, IHC staining with the HBC marker, TRP63, showed that the density of TRP63+ cells was significantly less in Upf3b-null OE than WT OE (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry quantification validating the scRNA-seq finding.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the relative proportion of GBCs, iOSNs, and mOSNs between Upf3b-null and WT mice.
claims.source: This effect appeared to be specific, as we observed no significant difference in the relative proportion of GBCs, iOSNs, and mOSNs between Upf3b-null and WT mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data comparing cell frequencies between genotypes.

claims.claim: There was a striking increase in the frequency of the mOSN-4 sub-cluster in Upf3b-null mice.
claims.source: Despite no significant effect on the mOSN stage as a whole (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), we observed a striking increase in the frequency of 1 of the 4 mOSN sub-clusters—mOSN-4—in Upf3b-null mice (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data comparing sub-cluster frequencies between genotypes.

claims.claim: The mOSN-4 sub-cluster represented <1% of all OSNs in most WT mice and increased by an average of 25-fold in Upf3b-null mice (p<0.05).
claims.source: This sub-cluster represented <1% of all OSNs in most WT mice and increased by an average of 25-fold in Upf3b-null mice (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of scRNA-seq data comparing sub-cluster frequencies.

claims.claim: Upf3b-null mice had an almost complete loss of the mOSN-2 sub-cluster.
claims.source: Conversely, Upf3b-null mice had an almost complete loss of another mOSN sub-cluster—mOSN-2—a sub-cluster that was populated by many cells in most WT mice (Figure 6B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data comparing sub-cluster frequencies between genotypes.

claims.claim: A major category of Upf3b-regulated genes in OSNs are immune genes, including a large fraction of genes encoding antimicrobial proteins.
claims.source: This revealed that a major category of Upf3b-regulated genes in OSNs are immune genes, including a large fraction of genes encoding antimicrobial proteins (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis identifying differentially expressed genes.

claims.claim: Most antimicrobial genes were expressed and upregulated in Upf3b-null mice at the HBC, GBC, and iOSNs stages.
claims.source: The expression of anti-microbial genes was not confined to the mature neurons in the OE (i.e. mOSNs), as we found that most of these immune-defense genes were also expressed and upregulated in Upf3b-null mice at the HBC, GBC, and iOSNs stages (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data showing antimicrobial gene expression across OSN developmental stages.

claims.claim: More than half (48 out of 88) of upregulated mRNAs encoding immune-related proteins harbor at least one NMD-inducing feature.
claims.source: More than half (48 out of 88) of these upregulated mRNAs encoding immune-related proteins harbor at least one NIF (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational analysis of NMD-inducing features in upregulated immune genes.

claims.claim: CAMP protein is expressed in the OE and is upregulated in Upf3b-null mice.
claims.source: To further assess its regulation, we performed western blot analysis with a validated anti-CAMP antiserum, which showed that CAMP protein is expressed in the OE and is upregulated in Upf3b-null mice (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is based on Western blot analysis of CAMP protein levels.

claims.claim: 78 Olfr genes are significantly downregulated in Upf3b-null mOSNs.
claims.source: In total, we identified 78 Olfr genes significantly downregulated in Upf3b-null mOSNs (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis of mOSNs.

claims.claim: The 78 Olfr genes downregulated in Upf3b-null mice are widely chromosomally distributed.
claims.source: We considered the possibility that these 78 Olfr genes are regulated by Upf3b through a common local cis-acting regulatory sequence, but against this hypothesis, we found that these 78 Olfr genes are widely chromosomally distributed (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of chromosomal locations of the 78 Olfr genes.

claims.claim: 490 of 3887 mOSNs in WT mice (13%) express one of the 78 downregulated Olfr genes as the dominant Olfr gene.
claims.source: We found that 490 of 3887 mOSNs in WT mice (13%) express one of these 78 Olfr genes as the dominant Olfr gene.
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis of Olfr gene expression in individual mOSNs.

claims.claim: Only 328 of 4654 mOSNs in Upf3b-null mice (7%) express one of the 78 downregulated Olfr genes as the dominant Olfr gene.
claims.source: In contrast, only 328 of 4654 mOSNs in Upf3b-null mice (7%) express one of these 78 Olfr genes as the dominant Olfr gene (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis of Olfr gene expression in individual mOSNs.

claims.claim: When all known Olfr genes were considered as a group, there was no significant difference in the percentage of Olfr genes selected in Upf3b-null vs. WT mOSNs.
claims.source: In contrast, when all known Olfr genes were considered as a group, there was no significant difference in the percentage of Olfr genes selected in Upf3b-null vs. WT mOSNs (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis of all Olfr gene expression in mOSNs.

claims.claim: The 78 downregulated Olfr genes were under-represented in Upf3b-null iOSNs as compared with WT iOSNs (5.6% vs 8.0%, p<0.05).
claims.source: Likewise, we found that these 78 Olfr genes were under-represented in Upf3b-null iOSNs as compared with WT iOSNs (5.6% vs 8.0%, p<0.05) (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis of Olfr gene expression in iOSNs.

claims.claim: Olfactory defects predict the later onset of numerous CNS disorders, including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.
claims.source: There is also considerable clinical interest in the olfactory system, as olfactory defects predict the later onset of numerous CNS disorders, including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease (Doty, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on olfactory dysfunction and CNS disorders.

claims.claim: Olfactory dysfunction strongly associates with autism.
claims.source: Olfactory dysfunction also strongly associates with autism (Rozenkrantz et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on olfactory dysfunction in autism.

claims.claim: Individual OSNs select a single Olfr gene for expression from the large repertoire of more than 1000 Olfr genes.
claims.source: There are more than 1000 olfactory receptor (Olfr) genes in mice (Zhang and Firestein, 2002). Individual OSNs select a single Olfr gene for expression from this large repertoire (Chess et al., 1994; Malnic et al., 1999; Serizawa et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies establishing the one-neuron-one-receptor rule.

claims.claim: Mafg and Irf8 encode transcriptional repressors that bind O/E consensus sites found in Olfr gene promoters.
claims.source: Both encode transcriptional repressors (Igarashi et al., 1994; Salem et al., 2014) that bind O/E consensus sites found in Olfr gene promoters (Michaloski et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Mafg and Irf8 function and DNA binding.

claims.claim: MAFG is a member of the Maf subfamily of basic leucine-zipper transcription factor genes that encode small proteins containing a B-ZAP DNA-binding domain but lack a transactivation domain.
claims.source: Mafg is a member of the Maf subfamily of basic leucine-zipper transcription factor genes that encode small proteins containing a B-ZAP DNA-binding domain, but lack a transactivation domain, and thus members of this family dimerize to form transcriptional repressors (Igarashi et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing MAFG structure and function.

claims.claim: MAFG is best known for its ability to regulate globin transcription in erythroid cells.
claims.source: MAFG is best known for its ability to regulate globin transcription in erythroid cells
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MAFG function.

claims.claim: IRF8 regulates the development of hematopoietic cells.
claims.source: IRF8 regulates the development hematopoietic cells
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about IRF8 function.

claims.claim: A recent study showed that inflammation causes OSNs to switch from a role in olfaction to immune defense.
claims.source: In support, a recent study showed that inflammation causes OSNs to switch from a role in olfaction to immune defense (Chen et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on OSN function during inflammation.

claims.claim: Upf2 conditional knockout in the murine forebrain leads to immune infiltration, coupled with deficits in memory, synaptic plasticity, social, and vocal communication.
claims.source: In particular, this study found that Upf2 conditional knockout in the murine forebrain leads to immune infiltration, coupled with deficits in memory, synaptic plasticity, social, and vocal communication (Johnson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Upf2 knockout effects in the brain.

claims.claim: Anti-inflammatory agents partially rescued many of the deficits in Upf2-conditional knockout mice.
claims.source: Importantly, they found that anti-inflammatory agents partially rescued many of these deficits, indicating that the inflammation is at least partially responsible for the neural defects in these Upf2-conditional knockout mice.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing rescue of Upf2 knockout phenotypes with anti-inflammatory treatment.

claims.claim: Some viruses have been shown to inhibit NMD, and NMD can inhibit viral infection.
claims.source: In this regard, it is notable that some viruses have been shown to inhibit NMD, and, in turn, NMD can inhibit viral infection (Wachter and Hartmann, 2014; Wada et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on virus-NMD interactions.

claims.claim: Notch2, Bhlhe40, and Rac2 are high-confidence NMD targets in mOSNs that encode factors previously shown to regulate the expression of many genes encoding inflammatory mediators and antimicrobial proteins.
claims.source: In particular, we identified three mRNAs—Notch2, Bhlhe40, and Rac2—which are high-confidence NMD targets in mOSNs (Table 1) that encode factors previously shown to regulate the expression of many genes encoding inflammatory mediators and antimicrobial proteins (Dooley et al., 2009; Jarjour et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on the study's NMD target identification and citations to studies on these factors' roles in immune regulation.

claims.claim: Upf3b-null mice have decreased numbers of HBCs.
claims.source: We found that Upf3b-null mice have decreased numbers of HBCs, suggesting that UPF3B promotes the maintenance of these reserve stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq and immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: UPF3B promotes the maintenance of HBCs.
claims.source: We found that Upf3b-null mice have decreased numbers of HBCs, suggesting that UPF3B promotes the maintenance of these reserve stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the decreased HBC numbers in Upf3b-null mice.

claims.claim: The mOSN-2 sub-cluster is likely to be functional based on enrichment of genes known to be essential for olfactory epithelium development and/or olfaction.
claims.source: The mOSN-2 sub-cluster is likely to be functional, as genes enriched in this sub-cluster include Pten, App, Cnga2, Nrp2, Ncam1, Adcy3, Gnal, Atf5, and Gfy (Supplementary file 4), all of which are known to be essential for olfactory epithelium development and/or olfaction.
claims.evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data showing enrichment of functionally important genes and knowledge of their roles.

claims.claim: Gdf11 functions in negative-feedback control of OE neurogenesis.
claims.source: For example, Gdf11 functions in negative-feedback control of OE neurogenesis
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Gdf11 function cited from the literature.

claims.claim: Lrp2 promotes the proliferation of neural precursor cells in the subependymal zone of the olfactory bulb.
claims.source: Lrp2 promotes the proliferation of neural precursor cells in the subependymal zone of the olfactory bulb
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Lrp2 function cited from the literature.

claims.claim: Notch2 is required for maintaining sustentacular cell function in the OE.
claims.source: Notch2 is required for maintaining sustentacular cell function in the OE (Gajera et al., 2010; Kawauchi et al., 2009; Rodriguez et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Notch2 function in the OE.

claims.claim: Ptch1 and Hk2 encode proteins known to be important for the development of neurons outside of the olfactory system.
claims.source: Other NMD target mRNAs that we identified, including Ptch1 and Hk2, encode proteins known to be important for the development of neurons outside of the olfactory system (Iulianella and Stanton-Turcotte, 2019; Zheng et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Ptch1 and Hk2 function in neural development.

claims.claim: The genes differentially expressed by the sub-clusters identified in this study suggest functional relevance of OSN heterogeneity.
claims.source: While we do not know the significance of this heterogeneity, the genes differentially expressed by the sub-clusters we identified suggests functional relevance.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential gene expression patterns observed in scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Translation is a highly energy-consuming process.
claims.source: Given that translation is a highly energy-consuming process (Lynch and Marinov, 2015), it is likely that there has been strong selection pressure for many mRNAs to be translated inefficiently.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on the energetic cost of translation.

claims.claim: Modestly translated mRNAs encode many key mOSN proteins, including receptors, signaling factors, and developmental regulators.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that modestly translated mRNAs encode many key mOSN proteins, including receptors, signaling factors, and developmental regulators.
claims.evidence: This is based on RiboTag and RNA-seq data analysis showing translation efficiency of different functional categories of genes.

claims.claim: NMD is a translation-dependent pathway based on protein-synthesis inhibitor and transfection experiments in immortalized cell lines.
claims.source: NMD is a translation-dependent pathway, based on protein-synthesis inhibitor and transfection experiments in immortalized cell lines (Belgrader et al., 1993; Carter et al., 1995; Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating NMD's dependence on translation.

claims.claim: UPF3B influences the selection of 78 specific Olfr genes to be the dominant Olfr gene expressed in individual mOSNs.
claims.source: Together, these results support a model in which UPF3B promotes the selection of these 78 Olfr genes to be the dominant Olfr gene expressed in individual mOSNs
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data showing both reduced expression and reduced frequency of these Olfr genes in individual cells.

claims.claim: OSNs function not only in olfaction but also in defense against microbes in the bronchial airways.
claims.source: This finding, coupled with our finding that OSNs constitutively express these anti-microbial genes (albeit at low levels), suggests that OSNs function not only in olfaction but also in defense against microbes in the bronchial airways.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the expression of antimicrobial genes in OSNs and their upregulation in Upf3b-null mice.

claims.claim: Loss of Upf3b may trigger OE inflammation, which diverts OSNs from functioning in olfaction to immune defense, thereby causing deficient olfaction.
claims.source: This raises the interesting possibility that loss of Upf3b triggers OE inflammation, which, in turn, diverts OSNs from functioning in olfaction to immune defense, thereby causing deficient olfaction.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the upregulation of immune genes and a cited study showing OSN functional switching during inflammation.

claims.claim: Humans with UPF3B mutations may suffer from neuro-inflammation that is responsible for their intellectual disability.
claims.source: It will be intriguing to determine whether humans with UPF3B mutations also suffer from neuro-inflammation and whether this is responsible for their intellectual disability.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on findings in Upf2 knockout mice and the known association of UPF3B mutations with intellectual disability.

claims.claim: The reason OSNs express high levels of antimicrobial genes in response to NMD inhibition may be to cope with infectious agents that inhibit NMD.
claims.source: Coupled with our data, these findings raise the intriguing possibility that the reason that OSNs express high levels of antimicrobial genes in response to NMD inhibition is because this provides a means to cope with infectious agents, particularly those that inhibit NMD as a means to avoid the antiviral actions of NMD.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting the study's findings with known virus-NMD interactions.

claims.claim: UPF3B loss may convert the mOSN-2 sub-cluster into the mOSN-4 sub-cluster.
claims.source: This reciprocal shift in these two mOSN sub-clusters in Upf3b-null mice raises the possibility that UPF3B loss converts the mOSN-2 sub-cluster into the mOSN-4 sub-cluster.
claims.evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the reciprocal changes in these two sub-clusters.

results.result: UPF3B is critical for human cognition and neural function. Mutations in UPF3B cause intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia, and ADHD in humans. Mouse models recapitulate behavioral and neural connectivity defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C22-C27 are well-supported by citations to human genetic studies and mouse model characterization. The evidence establishes UPF3B's importance in cognition through both human pedigree analysis and mouse behavioral/cellular studies.

results.result: Upf3b-null mice exhibit a partial olfactory defect characterized by postnatal weight deficit that resolves in adulthood and decreased expression of olfactory marker genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by weight measurements (Figure 1A), qPCR data (Figure 1B), and comparison to literature on olfactory-deficient mice. The temporal pattern of weight deficit is characteristic of partial olfactory defects.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis identified 235 differentially expressed genes in Upf3b-null mOSNs, with upregulated genes enriched for developmental functions and downregulated genes enriched for olfactory functions, particularly 78 Olfr genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2), qPCR validation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), and GO analysis. The statistical threshold (q<0.05) and validation strengthen these findings.

results.result: 52 high-confidence NMD target mRNAs were identified in mOSNs based on upregulation, stabilization, and presence of NMD-inducing features, with 11 overlapping previously known NMD targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 and C7 are supported by integrative computational analysis combining RNA-seq, RNA stability inference (REMBRANDTS), and NIF identification. The overlap with known targets validates the approach, though cell-type specificity explains limited overlap.

results.result: RiboTag analysis revealed that mOSN mRNAs with longer 3'UTRs (>2 kb) have higher translation efficiency, with highly translated mRNAs averaging ~1.8 kb 3'UTRs versus ~0.9 kb for lowly translated mRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 and C6 are supported by RiboTag experimental data (Figure 2B,C). The correlation between 3'UTR length and translation efficiency is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic basis requires further investigation.

results.result: NMD magnitude correlates with translation efficiency in vivo, with highly translated mRNAs showing stronger NMD response than lowly translated mRNAs, supporting that NMD is translation-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 and C101 are supported by integrated RNA-seq and RiboTag analysis (Figure 2F,G). The correlation (R²=0.5) for high-translation targets versus no correlation (R²=0.06) for low-translation targets provides strong evidence for translation-dependent NMD in vivo.

results.result: UPF3B loss has minimal global effects on translation efficiency, with only 16 of thousands of mOSN mRNAs showing significantly altered translation efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by RiboTag analysis (Figure 2H,I, Supplementary file 2). The scatter plot demonstrates that the vast majority of mRNAs remain on the diagonal, indicating preserved translation efficiency.

results.result: scRNA-seq analysis of 25,165 OE cells identified 16 cell types and revealed considerable heterogeneity within OSN populations, with multiple sub-clusters identified for HBCs, GBCs, iOSNs, and mOSNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C2 are supported by scRNA-seq data with appropriate quality control and UMAP clustering (Figure 3). The identification of sub-clusters is reproducible across biological replicates.

results.result: Cell cycle and pseudotime trajectory analyses revealed that HBCs are quiescent while GBCs are proliferative, GBC sub-clusters follow a linear developmental progression, and OSN development follows a HBC→GBC→iOSN→mOSN trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 are supported by cell cycle analysis (Figure 3F), Monocle trajectory analysis (Figures 4B, 5A), and consistency with previous studies. The developmental trajectory is well-established in the literature.

results.result: Upf3b-null mice have significantly reduced HBC frequency (p<0.05) as measured by scRNA-seq and validated by immunohistochemistry, suggesting UPF3B promotes HBC maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 and C91-C92 are supported by scRNA-seq quantification (Figure 6A) and IHC validation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). The inference that UPF3B promotes HBC maintenance is reasonable but requires functional validation.

results.result: There was no significant difference in the relative proportions of GBCs, iOSNs, and mOSNs between Upf3b-null and WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is based on scRNA-seq data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), but the authors acknowledge that variability among samples may have obscured subtle changes. The lack of statistical significance may reflect insufficient power rather than true absence of effect.

results.result: Upf3b loss causes a striking 25-fold increase in the mOSN-4 sub-cluster (p<0.05) and near-complete loss of the mOSN-2 sub-cluster, demonstrating that UPF3B influences specific OSN subsets.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 and C3 are supported by scRNA-seq data (Figure 6B,C). The reciprocal changes in these sub-clusters are dramatic and statistically significant for mOSN-4, though mOSN-2 reduction did not reach significance (p=0.24) due to sample variability.

results.result: UPF3B regulates expression of antimicrobial genes across OSN developmental stages, with over half (48/88) of upregulated immune-related mRNAs harboring NMD-inducing features.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C4 are supported by scRNA-seq differential expression analysis (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 5) and computational NIF analysis. The presence of NIFs in >50% of immune genes suggests direct NMD regulation.

results.result: CAMP protein is expressed in the OE and upregulated in Upf3b-null mice as demonstrated by Western blot and immunofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by Western blot quantification (Figure 6F) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B). The validation at protein level strengthens the RNA-seq findings.

results.result: UPF3B promotes selection of 78 specific Olfr genes as dominant receptors in individual mOSNs and iOSNs, with these genes showing reduced frequency in Upf3b-null cells (13% to 7% in mOSNs, 8% to 5.6% in iOSNs) while overall Olfr gene selection remains unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78, C5, and C102 are supported by integrated RNA-seq and scRNA-seq analysis (Figures 1C, 6H,I). The chromosomal distribution analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) argues against cis-regulatory mechanisms. The single-cell data demonstrating reduced frequency of these Olfr genes as dominant receptors is compelling.

results.result: Background on NMD pathway: NMD is a conserved RNA decay pathway that degrades aberrant and normal RNAs, involves >15 proteins including core factors UPF1/2/3, and consists of multiple branches with different mechanisms including EJC-dependent and EJC-independent pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C21 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the NMD literature. These are well-accepted facts in the field.

results.result: Background on olfactory system: The OE has lifelong neurogenic capacity, mOSNs develop via HBC→GBC→iOSN→mOSN pathway, HBCs are reserve stem cells, GBCs are active stem cells/progenitors, and mOSNs recognize odorants through various chemosensory receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 provide established background knowledge about the olfactory system supported by appropriate citations. These are well-accepted facts in the field.

results.result: Background on olfactory dysfunction: Olfactory defects predict onset of CNS disorders including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease and associate with autism. Individual OSNs select a single Olfr gene from >1000 genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The one-neuron-one-receptor rule is well-established.

results.result: Mafg and Irf8 encode transcriptional repressors that bind Olfr gene promoters. MAFG is a basic leucine-zipper transcription factor known for regulating globin transcription, while IRF8 regulates hematopoietic cell development.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by citations to studies characterizing these transcription factors. The connection to Olfr regulation is based on known DNA-binding specificity and upregulation in Upf3b-null mice.

results.result: Literature context for immune findings: Inflammation causes OSN functional switching to immune defense, Upf2 knockout causes neuro-inflammation rescued by anti-inflammatory agents, viruses inhibit NMD, and Notch2/Bhlhe40/Rac2 are NMD targets that regulate immune gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by appropriate citations and integration with the current study's findings. C90 combines data from this study (NMD target identification) with literature on immune regulation.

results.result: Functional context for identified NMD targets: The mOSN-2 sub-cluster is likely functional based on enrichment of genes essential for OE development/olfaction. Several identified NMD targets (Gdf11, Lrp2, Notch2, Ptch1, Hk2) have known roles in neurogenesis and neural development.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 are supported by scRNA-seq data showing gene enrichment (Supplementary file 4) and citations to literature on gene function. The inference of functionality is reasonable based on known gene roles.

results.result: Functional implications of OSN heterogeneity and translation: The differential gene expression in OSN sub-clusters suggests functional relevance. Translation is energy-consuming, and modestly translated mRNAs encode key mOSN proteins including receptors and developmental regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by scRNA-seq data analysis and RiboTag data (Figure 2D,E). The inference of functional relevance is reasonable but requires experimental validation.

results.result: Speculative models: OSNs may function in both olfaction and immune defense. Upf3b loss may trigger inflammation causing OSN functional switching and olfactory defects. Humans with UPF3B mutations may have neuro-inflammation. Antimicrobial gene expression may help cope with NMD-inhibiting pathogens. UPF3B loss may convert mOSN-2 to mOSN-4 sub-cluster.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are speculative models based on the study's findings and literature. While the reasoning is logical and supported by circumstantial evidence, these hypotheses require direct experimental testing. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than established facts.
